question: Vessel A (power-driven) sights Vessel B (power-driven) nearly abeam to port, bearing -70 degrees relative, with risk of collision, both in sight of one another. Who is give-way and what must each do?
gold_answer: Vessel B is the give-way vessel (Rule 15, since A is on B's starboard side) and must keep well clear, typically altering to starboard to pass astern of A. Vessel A is the stand-on vessel and must maintain course and speed under Rule 17(a)(i), only deviating under Rule 17(a)(ii)/(b) if B fails to act or collision becomes otherwise unavoidable.
expected_points: With B on A's port side, A is not the give-way vessel; the roles reverse relative to the previous starboard-bow examples.

question: Two power-driven vessels are approaching on reciprocal courses at night. Vessel A observes Vessel B dead ahead, masthead lights in line, both sidelights visible. What situation exists and what must each vessel do?
gold_answer: A head-on situation exists under Rule 14. Each vessel shall alter course to starboard so that each passes on the port side of the other; neither is 'stand-on'.
expected_points: Rule 14(a)-(b) - this is a mutual obligation, not a give-way/stand-on pairing.

question: Two power-driven vessels are approaching on reciprocal courses at night. Vessel A observes Vessel B nearly ahead, masthead lights nearly in line, both sidelights visible. What situation exists and what must each vessel do?
gold_answer: A head-on situation exists under Rule 14. Each vessel shall alter course to starboard so that each passes on the port side of the other; neither is 'stand-on'.
expected_points: Rule 14(a)-(b) - this is a mutual obligation, not a give-way/stand-on pairing.

question: Vessel A is uncertain whether Vessel B, approaching from nearly ahead at night, is on a reciprocal or a very slightly crossing course. What should Vessel A assume and do?
gold_answer: She shall assume a head-on situation exists and act accordingly, altering course to starboard.
expected_points: Rule 14(c) resolves doubt in favour of the head-on rule.

question: Vessel A is coming up on Vessel B from 30 degrees abaft her port beam, able to see only B's sternlight. What situation exists and who must keep clear?
gold_answer: An overtaking situation exists (Rule 13). Vessel A, the overtaking vessel, must keep out of the way of Vessel B until finally past and clear, regardless of B's category (power-driven or sailing).
expected_points: Rule 13 overrides the crossing/head-on rules and Rule 18 category order - it applies 'notwithstanding anything contained in Rules 4-18'.

question: Vessel A is coming up on Vessel B from 45 degrees abaft her starboard beam, able to see only B's sternlight. What situation exists and who must keep clear?
gold_answer: An overtaking situation exists (Rule 13). Vessel A, the overtaking vessel, must keep out of the way of Vessel B until finally past and clear, regardless of B's category (power-driven or sailing).
expected_points: Rule 13 overrides the crossing/head-on rules and Rule 18 category order - it applies 'notwithstanding anything contained in Rules 4-18'.

question: Vessel A is coming up on Vessel B from directly astern, able to see only B's sternlight. What situation exists and who must keep clear?
gold_answer: An overtaking situation exists (Rule 13). Vessel A, the overtaking vessel, must keep out of the way of Vessel B until finally past and clear, regardless of B's category (power-driven or sailing).
expected_points: Rule 13 overrides the crossing/head-on rules and Rule 18 category order - it applies 'notwithstanding anything contained in Rules 4-18'.

question: Vessel A is 20 degrees abaft Vessel B's beam, close to the 22.5-degree threshold, and cannot be certain whether she is overtaking or crossing. What should she assume?
gold_answer: She shall assume it is an overtaking situation and keep clear of Vessel B accordingly.
expected_points: Rule 13(c) resolves ambiguity in favour of overtaking, which imposes the stricter duty (keep clear until finally past and clear, not just avoid crossing ahead).

question: Two power-driven vessels are approaching each other in dense fog and are not visible to one another, only detected by radar, on courses that would be head-on if they were in sight. Do Rules 14 (head-on) or 15 (crossing) apply?
gold_answer: No - Rules 11-18 (including Rule 14/15) apply only to vessels in sight of one another (Rule 11). In restricted visibility with no visual sighting, Rule 19 (conduct in restricted visibility) applies instead.
expected_points: This is a key exam trap: radar contact does not equal 'in sight' for Section II purposes.

question: Vessel B is the stand-on vessel in a crossing situation but Vessel A (give-way) has taken no avoiding action and the range is closing rapidly. What may/must Vessel B do?
gold_answer: Under Rule 17(a)(ii), B may take action to avoid collision by her own manoeuvre as soon as it becomes apparent A is not taking appropriate action. If collision cannot be avoided by A's action alone, Rule 17(b) requires B to take such action as will best aid to avoid collision.
expected_points: Rule 17 escalates the stand-on vessel's discretion into an obligation as the situation deteriorates.

question: Vessel B (stand-on, power-driven) is in a crossing situation with Vessel A on B's own port side and must take action under Rule 17(a)(ii). Why should B generally avoid altering to port in this case?
gold_answer: Because Rule 17(c) provides that, if she has room, she should not alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side, since that could turn her toward the other vessel or create confusion; a starboard alteration or reduction of speed is generally preferred.
expected_points: Rule 17(c) specifically addresses this to avoid worsening the situation.

question: Two sailing vessels, A and B, are approaching with risk of collision. A has the wind on the port side, B has the wind on the starboard side. Who keeps out of the way?
gold_answer: A must keep out of the way of B.
expected_points: Rule 12(a): port-tack gives way to starboard-tack; when on the same tack, windward gives way to leeward.

question: Two sailing vessels, A and B, are approaching with risk of collision. Both A and B have the wind on the port side and A is to windward of B. Who keeps out of the way?
gold_answer: A (to windward) must keep out of the way of B (to leeward).
expected_points: Rule 12(a): port-tack gives way to starboard-tack; when on the same tack, windward gives way to leeward.

question: Two sailing vessels, A and B, are approaching with risk of collision. Both A and B have the wind on the starboard side and B is to windward of A. Who keeps out of the way?
gold_answer: B (to windward) must keep out of the way of A (to leeward).
expected_points: Rule 12(a): port-tack gives way to starboard-tack; when on the same tack, windward gives way to leeward.

question: An ordinary power-driven vessel underway meets a vessel not under command with risk of collision, both in sight of one another, not in a narrow channel or TSS crossing situation, and not an overtaking case. Who keeps out of the way?
gold_answer: The power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, per the Rule 18(a) hierarchy.
expected_points: Rule 18(a) ranks NUC and RAM vessels, fishing vessels and sailing vessels all above an ordinary power-driven vessel.

question: An ordinary power-driven vessel underway meets a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre with risk of collision, both in sight of one another, not in a narrow channel or TSS crossing situation, and not an overtaking case. Who keeps out of the way?
gold_answer: The power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, per the Rule 18(a) hierarchy.
expected_points: Rule 18(a) ranks NUC and RAM vessels, fishing vessels and sailing vessels all above an ordinary power-driven vessel.

question: An ordinary power-driven vessel underway meets a vessel engaged in fishing (nets out, restricted manoeuvrability) with risk of collision, both in sight of one another, not in a narrow channel or TSS crossing situation, and not an overtaking case. Who keeps out of the way?
gold_answer: The power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a vessel engaged in fishing (nets out, restricted manoeuvrability), per the Rule 18(a) hierarchy.
expected_points: Rule 18(a) ranks NUC and RAM vessels, fishing vessels and sailing vessels all above an ordinary power-driven vessel.

question: An ordinary power-driven vessel underway meets a sailing vessel under sail alone with risk of collision, both in sight of one another, not in a narrow channel or TSS crossing situation, and not an overtaking case. Who keeps out of the way?
gold_answer: The power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a sailing vessel under sail alone, per the Rule 18(a) hierarchy.
expected_points: Rule 18(a) ranks NUC and RAM vessels, fishing vessels and sailing vessels all above an ordinary power-driven vessel.

question: A power-driven vessel is overtaking a sailing vessel from a position more than 22.5 degrees abaft the sailing vessel's beam. Which rule governs - Rule 13 (overtaking) or Rule 18 (responsibilities, which would otherwise make the power-driven vessel give way to the sailing vessel anyway)?
gold_answer: Rule 13 governs. It applies 'notwithstanding anything contained in Rules 4-18', so the power-driven (overtaking) vessel must keep clear as the overtaking vessel, though in this case the outcome (power gives way) happens to coincide with Rule 18's usual order.
expected_points: The teaching point is that Rule 13 takes precedence over the category hierarchy of Rule 18 in all overtaking situations, including where it would reverse the normal Rule 18 outcome (e.g., a fishing vessel overtaking a power-driven vessel must keep clear as overtaker, despite outranking power-driven vessels under Rule 18(a)(iii)).

question: A vessel engaged in fishing is overtaking an ordinary power-driven vessel from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the power-driven vessel's beam. Rule 18 would normally require the power-driven vessel to give way to the fishing vessel. Which rule actually applies, and who gives way?
gold_answer: Rule 13 applies because this is an overtaking situation, and it overrides Rule 18. The fishing vessel, as the overtaking vessel, must keep out of the way of the power-driven vessel being overtaken.
expected_points: This is a commonly-tested exception showing Rule 13's precedence over the Rule 18 hierarchy.

question: Vessel A (give-way, power-driven) is crossing with Vessel B (stand-on) on A's starboard bow. A third vessel, C, is also in sight, ahead of A on a steady bearing. How should A's Rule 16 action account for C?
gold_answer: A's action to comply with Rule 16 (avoid B) must also comply with Rule 8(d)/(f) - it must not create a close-quarters situation or risk of collision with C. A should choose an alteration (typically to starboard, astern of B) that keeps her clear of both B and C simultaneously; if no single safe manoeuvre exists, A should reduce speed or stop under Rule 8(e) while reassessing.
expected_points: Real traffic situations require considering all vessels in sight together, not resolving encounters pairwise in isolation.

question: In a head-on encounter under Rule 14, is there a 'stand-on' vessel that should hold course and speed?
gold_answer: No - Rule 14 imposes a mutual obligation on both vessels to alter course to starboard; there is no stand-on vessel and Rule 17 does not apply to a head-on situation.
expected_points: This distinguishes Rule 14 (mutual duty) from Rules 15 and 13 (give-way/stand-on pairs).

question: Vessel A is the give-way vessel in a crossing situation. She alters course only 5 degrees to starboard at long range. Does this satisfy Rules 8(b) and 16?
gold_answer: Likely not - Rule 8(b) requires alterations to be large enough to be readily apparent to the other vessel by radar or visually, and Rule 16 requires early and substantial action; a 5-degree change is unlikely to be perceptible or substantial enough.
expected_points: Exam scenarios frequently test the 'large enough to be apparent' standard as distinct from merely 'some' action.

question: To which vessels does Rule 19 apply?
gold_answer: To vessels not in sight of one another when navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility.
expected_points: Rule 19(a).

question: What must every vessel do under Rule 19(b)?
gold_answer: Proceed at a safe speed adapted to the prevailing circumstances and conditions of restricted visibility; a power-driven vessel shall have her engines ready for immediate manoeuvre.
expected_points: Rule 19(b).

question: What must every vessel do under Rule 19(c) when complying with Section I rules?
gold_answer: Have due regard to the prevailing circumstances and conditions of restricted visibility.
expected_points: Rule 19(c) ties back to Rules 4-10.

question: A vessel detects another only by radar in restricted visibility and determines risk of collision exists. What must she do under Rule 19(d)?
gold_answer: Take avoiding action in ample time, provided that when such action consists of an alteration of course, so far as possible the following shall be avoided: (i) an alteration of course to port for a vessel forward of the beam, other than for a vessel being overtaken; and (ii) an alteration of course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.
expected_points: Rule 19(d) - these are specific prohibited manoeuvres unique to restricted visibility, since the other vessel cannot be seen and her aspect/intentions cannot be visually confirmed.

question: Why does Rule 19(d)(i) prohibit altering to port for a radar contact forward of the beam?
gold_answer: Because without visual contact, the other vessel's heading is unknown; altering to port could turn the vessel directly into the path of a contact that (unknown to the observer) may itself be turning to starboard as required, risking a collision instead of avoiding one.
expected_points: This rule exists because Rule 14/15 visual sighting cues are unavailable in restricted visibility.

question: What must a vessel do under Rule 19(e) if a fog signal is heard forward of her beam, or if a close-quarters situation with a vessel forward of the beam cannot be avoided?
gold_answer: She shall reduce her speed to the minimum at which she can be kept on her course; if necessary, take all her way off; and in any event navigate with extreme caution until the risk of collision is over.
expected_points: Rule 19(e) - this applies regardless of whether the contact is detected by radar or by hearing a fog signal.

question: In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel underway and making way sounds what signal, and at what interval?
gold_answer: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
expected_points: Rule 35(a).

question: What signal does a power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way through the water sound in restricted visibility?
gold_answer: Two prolonged blasts in succession, with an interval of about 2 seconds between them, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
expected_points: Rule 35(b).

question: What sound signal is given by a vessel not under command, restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, constrained by her draught, sailing, engaged in fishing, or towing/pushing (when underway), under Rule 35(c)?
gold_answer: One prolonged followed by two short blasts, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
expected_points: Rule 35(c).

question: What signal does a vessel at anchor sound in restricted visibility, and how often?
gold_answer: Rapid ringing of the bell for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute; a vessel of 100 metres or more shall sound the bell in the forepart and immediately after, a gong in the after part.
expected_points: Rule 35(f); additionally she may sound one short, one prolonged and one short blast to give warning of her position/possible collision risk (Rule 35(g)).

question: What signal does a vessel aground sound in restricted visibility?
gold_answer: The anchor bell signal, plus three separate and distinct strokes on the bell immediately before and after the rapid ringing; she may also sound an appropriate whistle signal.
expected_points: Rule 35(h).

question: Is a vessel under 12 metres in length required to give the signals of Rule 35?
gold_answer: No, but if she does not, she must make some other efficient sound signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
expected_points: Rule 35(i).

question: A vessel constrained by her draught detects, by radar only, another vessel crossing ahead in restricted visibility with risk of collision. What manoeuvre restriction under Rule 19(d) applies to her?
gold_answer: She should, so far as possible, avoid altering course to port for the vessel forward of her beam (unless she is overtaking) and avoid altering towards a vessel abeam or abaft her beam.
expected_points: Rule 19(d) applies to all vessel types, including CBD, when acting on radar detection alone.

question: Two vessels are in restricted visibility, each detecting the other only by radar on a steady bearing forward of the beam (a converging/'crossing-like' geometry). Neither vessel can see the other. Should either apply Rule 15's 'stand on'/'give way' roles?
gold_answer: No - Rules 15 and 17 (stand-on obligations) do not apply, because Section II requires the vessels to be in sight of one another; Rule 19 governs instead, with both vessels obliged to take early, ample avoiding action while observing the Rule 19(d) restrictions.
expected_points: There is no stand-on vessel in restricted visibility encounters, unlike Rule 15 crossing situations.

question: A vessel hears, apparently forward of her beam, the fog signal of another vessel, but cannot establish that risk of collision does not exist. What must she do?
gold_answer: Reduce her speed to the minimum at which she can be kept on her course, and if necessary take all way off, navigating with extreme caution until the danger of collision is over (Rule 19(e)).
expected_points: The trigger is inability to be certain that no risk of collision exists, not certainty that risk does exist.

question: Why does Rule 19 not have separate 'give-way' and 'stand-on' roles the way Rules 14/15 do?
gold_answer: Because vessels are not in sight of one another; without visual confirmation of the other's aspect, heading and actions, a fixed stand-on/give-way pairing could cause both vessels to unknowingly worsen the situation, so both share mutual duties to take early, cautious, and compliant avoiding action.
expected_points: This is a key conceptual distinction tested in COLREG exams.

question: Under Rule 19(b), what specific readiness must a power-driven vessel maintain in restricted visibility?
gold_answer: Her engines shall be ready for immediate manoeuvre.
expected_points: Rule 19(b).

question: A vessel is proceeding at a speed that would allow her to stop within half the distance of visibility. Does this automatically satisfy the 'safe speed' requirement of Rule 19(b)?
gold_answer: Not necessarily - 'half the distance of visibility' is a traditional rule of thumb but the Rule 6 factors (traffic density, manoeuvrability, radar characteristics, etc.) must all be considered; a numerically 'safe stopping distance' speed can still be unsafe given traffic density or manoeuvring limitations.
expected_points: Exam answers should reference the full Rule 6 factor list rather than a single rule of thumb.

question: A vessel altering course in restricted visibility to avoid a radar contact abaft her beam turns toward that contact. Is this compliant with Rule 19(d)(ii)?
gold_answer: No - Rule 19(d)(ii) requires avoiding, so far as possible, an alteration of course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.
expected_points: This is one of the two specific prohibited-manoeuvre patterns under Rule 19(d).

question: Is an alteration of course to port ever permitted under Rule 19(d) for a vessel forward of the beam?
gold_answer: Yes, if that vessel is being overtaken - the prohibition on altering to port for a vessel forward of the beam explicitly excludes the overtaking case.
expected_points: Rule 19(d)(i) carve-out.

question: How often must a vessel towed (if manned) sound her signal in restricted visibility, and what is it?
gold_answer: Immediately after the towing vessel's signal, she shall sound four blasts in succession, namely one prolonged followed by three short blasts, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
expected_points: Rule 35(e).

question: What signal does a pilot vessel engaged on pilotage duty sound in restricted visibility, in addition to or instead of other prescribed signals?
gold_answer: She may, in addition to the signals prescribed for her length/type, sound an identity signal of four short blasts.
expected_points: Rule 35(j).

question: Vessel A, in fog, detects Vessel B by radar 30 degrees forward of her port beam on a steady bearing with decreasing range; A and B are not overtaking. What alterations should A avoid, per Rule 19(d)?
gold_answer: A should avoid altering course to port (since B is forward of her beam and this is not an overtaking case) and should avoid altering towards B if B were instead abeam or abaft the beam (not applicable here since B is forward). A safe option would typically be an alteration to starboard and/or reduction of speed.
expected_points: Rule 19(d)(i) directly governs this geometry.

question: Vessel A, in fog, detects Vessel B by radar fine on her starboard quarter (abaft the beam), closing steadily. What should A avoid under Rule 19(d)(ii)?
gold_answer: A should avoid altering course towards B, i.e., avoid turning to starboard toward the quarter where B is located; reducing speed and/or altering away (to port, since B is abaft the beam so the port-alteration restriction of 19(d)(i) does not apply here) are safer options.
expected_points: Rule 19(d)(ii) governs contacts abeam/abaft the beam.

question: When must the Part C lights be exhibited?
gold_answer: From sunset to sunrise, and during such times no other lights shall be exhibited except such lights as cannot be mistaken for the prescribed lights, do not impair their visibility or distinctive character, or interfere with keeping a proper look-out.
expected_points: Rule 20(a)-(b).

question: When must shapes be exhibited?
gold_answer: By day.
expected_points: Rule 20(c).

question: Are the Rule 20 lights to be shown in restricted visibility during daytime, and in all other circumstances when deemed necessary?
gold_answer: Yes - the lights prescribed shall, if carried, also be exhibited from sunrise to sunset in restricted visibility and may be exhibited in all other circumstances when it is deemed necessary.
expected_points: Rule 20(d).

question: Define 'masthead light'.
gold_answer: A white light placed over the fore-and-aft centreline of the vessel showing an unbroken light over an arc of the horizon of 225 degrees, fixed so as to show from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side.
expected_points: Rule 21(a).

question: Define 'sidelights' and their arcs.
gold_answer: A green light on the starboard side and a red light on the port side, each showing an unbroken light over 112.5 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on their respective side.
expected_points: Rule 21(b).

question: Define 'sternlight'.
gold_answer: A white light placed as nearly as practicable at the stern, showing an unbroken light over an arc of 135 degrees, fixed to show 67.5 degrees from right aft on each side.
expected_points: Rule 21(c).

question: Define 'towing light'.
gold_answer: A yellow light having the same characteristics as the sternlight (135-degree arc, 67.5 degrees each side of right aft).
expected_points: Rule 21(d).

question: Define 'all-round light'.
gold_answer: A light showing an unbroken light over an arc of the horizon of 360 degrees.
expected_points: Rule 21(e).

question: Define 'flashing light'.
gold_answer: A light flashing at regular intervals at a frequency of 120 flashes or more per minute.
expected_points: Rule 21(f).

question: What is the minimum visibility range for a masthead light on a vessel of 50 metres or more in length?
gold_answer: 6 nautical miles.
expected_points: Rule 22(a)(i).

question: What is the minimum visibility range for a masthead light on a vessel of 12 metres but less than 50 metres in length?
gold_answer: 5 nautical miles (3 miles if the vessel is less than 20 metres in length).
expected_points: Rule 22(b)(i).

question: What is the minimum visibility range for sidelights on a vessel 50 m or more in length?
gold_answer: 3 nautical miles.
expected_points: Rule 22(a)(ii).

question: What is the minimum visibility range for a sternlight on a vessel of any length category down to less than 12 metres?
gold_answer: 2 nautical miles (vessels under 12 m); 2 nm sternlight also applies generally to smaller categories, while vessels 12-50 m require 2 nm sternlight as well.
expected_points: Rule 22(b)(iii)/(c)(iii).

question: What is the minimum visibility range for an all-round light on a vessel less than 12 metres in length?
gold_answer: 2 nautical miles.
expected_points: Rule 22(c)(iv).

question: What lights must a power-driven vessel underway (50 m or more) exhibit?
gold_answer: A masthead light forward; a second masthead light abaft of and higher than the forward one; sidelights; and a sternlight.
expected_points: Rule 23(a) - the two masthead lights give the 'range lights' used to judge aspect and closing.

question: May a power-driven vessel less than 12 metres in length exhibit an all-round white light in lieu of the masthead light and sternlight?
gold_answer: Yes, and she may also, if practicable, exhibit sidelights combined in one lantern carried on the fore-and-aft centreline.
expected_points: Rule 23(c) / (d) for vessels under 12 m and under 7 m at limited speed.

question: What additional light must an air-cushion vessel (hovercraft) operating in the non-displacement mode exhibit?
gold_answer: An all-round flashing yellow light.
expected_points: Rule 23(b).

question: What lights must a power-driven vessel towing astern exhibit if the length of the tow measured from the stern of the towing vessel to the back of the tow exceeds 200 metres?
gold_answer: Three masthead lights in a vertical line (instead of the normal one or two), plus sidelights, a sternlight, a towing light above the sternlight, and a diamond shape where it can best be seen.
expected_points: Rule 24(a).

question: What lights must a vessel or object being towed astern exhibit (manned)?
gold_answer: Sidelights, a sternlight, and if the length of the tow exceeds 200 metres, a diamond shape.
expected_points: Rule 24(e)/(g).

question: What lights does a power-driven vessel pushing ahead or towing alongside (as part of a composite unit) exhibit?
gold_answer: Two masthead lights in a vertical line (instead of the normal forward masthead light) at the fore end, sidelights, and a sternlight; if the vessels are rigidly connected as a composite unit they are lit as a single power-driven vessel.
expected_points: Rule 24(b)-(c).

question: What lights must a sailing vessel underway exhibit?
gold_answer: Sidelights and a sternlight (but not the masthead light).
expected_points: Rule 25(a).

question: What may a sailing vessel less than 20 metres in length exhibit combined in one lantern?
gold_answer: The sidelights and sternlight may be combined in one tricolour lantern at or near the masthead.
expected_points: Rule 25(b).

question: What optional lights may a sailing vessel exhibit at or near the top of the mast under Rule 25(c)?
gold_answer: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, the upper red and the lower green, but these shall not be exhibited in conjunction with the combined tricolour lantern.
expected_points: Rule 25(c).

question: What lights/shape must a vessel under sail also propelled by machinery (a motor-sailer) exhibit?
gold_answer: Forward, where it can best be seen, a conical shape, apex downward, since when under power she is legally a power-driven vessel and must also show power-driven vessel lights.
expected_points: Rule 25(e).

question: What lights may a sailing vessel/vessel under oars less than 7 metres show if the prescribed lights cannot practicably be exhibited?
gold_answer: She shall have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light, to be exhibited in sufficient time to prevent collision.
expected_points: Rule 25(d)(ii) also applies to vessels under oars.

question: What lights/shapes does a vessel engaged in trawling exhibit?
gold_answer: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, the upper green and the lower white (or a basket shape by day); when making way, also sidelights and a sternlight.
expected_points: Rule 26(b).

question: What lights/shapes does a vessel engaged in fishing other than trawling exhibit?
gold_answer: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, the upper red and the lower white (or two cones apex to apex vertically arranged by day); if outlying gear extends more than 150 metres, an additional all-round white light in the direction of the gear; when making way, also sidelights and a sternlight.
expected_points: Rule 26(c).

question: What lights/shapes does a vessel not under command exhibit?
gold_answer: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line where they can best be seen, and, if making way through the water, additionally sidelights and a sternlight; by day, two balls in a vertical line.
expected_points: Rule 27(a)/(b).

question: What lights/shapes does a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre exhibit (general case)?
gold_answer: Three all-round lights in a vertical line - red, white, red (top to bottom); by day, a ball, diamond, ball in a vertical line; if making way, also masthead light(s), sidelights and sternlight.
expected_points: Rule 27(b).

question: What additional shapes/lights does a RAM vessel engaged in dredging or underwater operations, with an obstruction, exhibit to indicate the safe side to pass?
gold_answer: Two all-round red lights or two balls in a vertical line to show the side on which the obstruction exists, and two all-round green lights or two diamonds in a vertical line to show the side on which another vessel may pass.
expected_points: Rule 27(d).

question: What signal must a vessel engaged in a towing operation which severely restricts her and her tow's ability to deviate exhibit, in addition to the RAM lights?
gold_answer: The lights or shapes prescribed for a vessel engaged in towing (Rule 24).
expected_points: Rule 27(c).

question: What lights/shape may a power-driven vessel constrained by her draught exhibit, in addition to those for power-driven vessels?
gold_answer: Three all-round red lights in a vertical line where they can best be seen, or a cylinder, by day.
expected_points: Rule 28.

question: What lights/shape does a vessel engaged on pilotage duty exhibit?
gold_answer: At or near the masthead, two all-round lights in a vertical line, the upper white and the lower red; when underway, also sidelights and a sternlight; when at anchor, additionally the anchor light(s); by day, she does not need a special shape but exhibits her identity signal as appropriate.
expected_points: Rule 29(a).

question: What lights does a vessel at anchor exhibit, if less than 50 metres in length?
gold_answer: An all-round white light where it can best be seen.
expected_points: Rule 30(a)(i)/(b).

question: What lights does a vessel at anchor 50 metres or more in length exhibit?
gold_answer: An all-round white light forward and another aft, at a lower level than the forward one, and, if 100 metres or more in length, use available deck lighting to illuminate her decks.
expected_points: Rule 30(a)-(c).

question: What shape does a vessel at anchor exhibit by day?
gold_answer: One ball where it can best be seen.
expected_points: Rule 30(a)(ii).

question: What lights/shapes does a vessel aground exhibit?
gold_answer: The anchor lights/ball as appropriate to her length, plus two all-round red lights in a vertical line, and by day three balls in a vertical line.
expected_points: Rule 30(d).

question: Is a vessel less than 7 metres in length, at anchor in a small craft/non-fairway area, required to exhibit the anchor light/shape?
gold_answer: No - she is not required to exhibit the anchor lights or shapes prescribed, unless anchored in or near a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or where other vessels normally navigate.
expected_points: Rule 30(e) grants a limited exemption for small vessels in defined circumstances.

question: What is required of a seaplane that cannot comply with Part C lights/shapes due to her construction?
gold_answer: She shall exhibit lights and shapes as closely similar in characteristics and position as is possible.
expected_points: Rule 31.

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line at night, no other lights visible. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: She is a vessel not under command, not making way (no sidelights/sternlight shown).
expected_points: Rule 27(a).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Two all-round red lights vertical, plus sidelights and a sternlight. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel not under command that is making way through the water.
expected_points: Rule 27(a)(ii) adds sidelights/sternlight when making way.

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Red-white-red all-round lights in a vertical line, plus sidelights and sternlight. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre that is making way through the water.
expected_points: Rule 27(b).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Ball, diamond, ball shapes in a vertical line by day. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre.
expected_points: Rule 27(b) day shapes.

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Three all-round red lights in a vertical line, shown in addition to normal power-driven vessel lights. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A power-driven vessel constrained by her draught.
expected_points: Rule 28.

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: A cylinder shape shown by day. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel constrained by her draught.
expected_points: Rule 28 day shape.

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Two all-round lights, upper green lower white, plus sidelights and sternlight while making way. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel engaged in trawling, making way through the water.
expected_points: Rule 26(b).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: A shape resembling two cones apex to apex, shown vertically by day. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel engaged in fishing (other than trawling).
expected_points: Rule 26(c) day shape.

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Two all-round lights, upper red lower white, plus an additional all-round white light in the direction of outlying gear more than 150 m away. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel engaged in fishing (other than trawling) with gear extending more than 150 metres.
expected_points: Rule 26(c)(ii).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: A white all-round light shown forward and a lower white all-round light shown aft, no other lights, vessel stationary. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel at anchor, 50 metres or more in length.
expected_points: Rule 30(a).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: A single all-round white light only, vessel stationary. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel at anchor, less than 50 metres in length.
expected_points: Rule 30(b).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Anchor lights/shape plus two all-round red lights in a vertical line. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel aground.
expected_points: Rule 30(d).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Three balls in a vertical line shown by day, vessel stationary. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel aground.
expected_points: Rule 30(d) day shape.

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Masthead light, second (higher, after) masthead light, sidelights, sternlight. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: An ordinary power-driven vessel underway, 50 metres or more in length.
expected_points: Rule 23(a).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: A single all-round white light only, vessel making way (small craft). What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A power-driven vessel underway, less than 12 metres in length, showing the permitted all-round light in lieu of masthead/sternlight.
expected_points: Rule 23(c)(i).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Sidelights and sternlight only, no masthead light. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A sailing vessel underway (or a vessel under oars showing the equivalent).
expected_points: Rule 25(a).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: A single tricolour lantern at the masthead combining red, green and white. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A sailing vessel under 20 metres exhibiting the combined lantern option.
expected_points: Rule 25(b).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, upper red, lower green, at the masthead, sidelights and sternlight also shown separately. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A sailing vessel exhibiting the optional Rule 25(c) lights (not combined with the tricolour lantern).
expected_points: Rule 25(c).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: A conical shape, apex down, shown forward by day on a vessel under both sail and power. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel proceeding under sail when also being propelled by machinery (motor-sailer, legally a power-driven vessel).
expected_points: Rule 25(e).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Two all-round white lights in a vertical line, upper and lower, at or near the masthead, plus sidelights and sternlight while underway. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A vessel engaged on pilotage duty, underway.
expected_points: Rule 29(a).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: An all-round flashing yellow light shown by a vessel moving fast and low over the water in non-displacement mode. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: An air-cushion vessel (hovercraft) operating in the non-displacement mode.
expected_points: Rule 23(b).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Three masthead lights in a vertical line on the towing vessel, instead of the usual one or two. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: A power-driven vessel towing astern where the length of tow exceeds 200 metres.
expected_points: Rule 24(a)(i).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: A diamond shape shown by the towing vessel and/or the vessel/object towed. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: Indicates the length of the tow exceeds 200 metres.
expected_points: Rule 24(a)(iv)/(g).

question: At night/by day you observe the following on a vessel: Two all-round red lights (or two balls) shown on one side, two all-round green lights (or two diamonds) on the other side of a RAM vessel. What is the vessel's status?
gold_answer: She is engaged in dredging/underwater operations with an obstruction; red side = danger side, green side = safe passing side.
expected_points: Rule 27(d).

question: Why are minimum light visibility ranges scaled to vessel length in Rule 22?
gold_answer: Larger vessels need to be detectable and identifiable from a greater distance because their size, momentum, and manoeuvring/stopping constraints require other vessels to have more time to assess and react.
expected_points: Rule 22 sets tiered minimum ranges (e.g., 6 nm masthead light for vessels 50 m+, 3 nm for smaller craft).

question: A 40-metre power-driven vessel shows only one masthead light instead of two. Is this compliant?
gold_answer: Yes, provided she is less than 50 metres in length - Rule 23(a) requires a second masthead light only on vessels 50 metres or more in length (a second may optionally be carried on smaller vessels but is not mandatory).
expected_points: Rule 23(a)(ii) makes the second masthead light optional below 50 m.

question: How can an observer distinguish a trawler from a vessel fishing with other gear at night, purely by colour of the upper light?
gold_answer: A trawler's upper light is green; a vessel fishing other than trawling shows an upper light that is red.
expected_points: Rule 26(b) vs 26(c) - 'green for trawling, red for other fishing' upper light colour.

question: What is the key visual difference at night between a 'vessel not under command' and a 'vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre'?
gold_answer: NUC shows two all-round red lights in a vertical line; RAM shows three all-round lights in a vertical line, red-white-red.
expected_points: The middle white light is the distinguishing feature of RAM versus NUC.

question: A 120-metre vessel is at anchor at night. Besides the forward and after anchor lights, what else is required?
gold_answer: She must use the available working or equivalent lights to illuminate her decks, since she is 100 metres or more in length.
expected_points: Rule 30(c).

question: A power-driven vessel is towing another vessel alongside (not astern), and the combination is not rigidly connected as a composite unit. What lights does the towing vessel show at her fore end?
gold_answer: Two masthead lights in a vertical line, in place of the light prescribed in Rule 23(a)(i), together with sidelights and a sternlight, and a towing light.
expected_points: Rule 24(c).

question: Why is the masthead light's arc set at 225 degrees rather than 360 degrees?
gold_answer: It is designed to be visible only over the forward arc (from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on each side) so that another vessel observing it can judge that the source vessel is approaching from roughly that direction, distinguishing an approaching vessel from one that is moving away (sternlight only).
expected_points: The masthead/sidelight/sternlight arc system lets an observer infer a vessel's aspect (approaching, crossing, or moving away) purely from which lights are visible.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: Define 'short blast' and 'prolonged blast'.
gold_answer: A short blast means a blast of about 1 second's duration. A prolonged blast means a blast of from 4 to 6 seconds' duration.
expected_points: Rule 32(b)-(c).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What sound signalling equipment must a vessel of 12 metres or more in length carry?
gold_answer: A whistle and a bell, and a vessel of 100 metres or more in length shall additionally carry a gong, the tone and sound of which cannot be confused with that of the bell.
expected_points: Rule 33(a).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: Is a vessel less than 12 metres in length required to carry the sound signalling appliances of Rule 33?
gold_answer: No, but if she does not, she must be provided with some other means of making an efficient sound signal.
expected_points: Rule 33(b).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What sound/light signal means 'I am altering my course to starboard'?
gold_answer: One short blast, optionally accompanied by one flash of a light.
expected_points: Rule 34(a)/(b).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What sound/light signal means 'I am altering my course to port'?
gold_answer: Two short blasts, optionally accompanied by two flashes of a light.
expected_points: Rule 34(a)/(b).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What sound/light signal means 'I am operating astern propulsion'?
gold_answer: Three short blasts, optionally accompanied by three flashes of a light.
expected_points: Rule 34(a)/(b).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What signal is given by a vessel that fails to understand the intentions or actions of another, or is in doubt whether sufficient action is being taken to avoid collision?
gold_answer: At least five short and rapid blasts on the whistle - the danger/doubt signal - which may be supplemented by at least five short and rapid flashes of a light.
expected_points: Rule 34(d).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What signal must a vessel approaching a bend or an area of a channel/fairway where other vessels may be obscured sound?
gold_answer: One prolonged blast.
expected_points: Rule 34(e).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: If a vessel hears the one-prolonged-blast bend signal, what should she do in response?
gold_answer: Answer with one prolonged blast.
expected_points: Rule 34(e).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What signals are given by two power-driven vessels in sight of one another when meeting/crossing and one is altering course, per Rule 34(a)?
gold_answer: Whistle signals indicate the course alteration being carried out: one short blast (starboard), two short blasts (port), three short blasts (astern propulsion).
expected_points: Rule 34(a) - these are action signals, not proposal/request signals, under the international Rules (unlike in some inland rules regimes).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What light characteristics apply to the manoeuvring light used with whistle signals under Rule 34(b)?
gold_answer: An all-round white light, visible at a minimum range of 5 miles, synchronised with the whistle and flashed for about 1 second per flash, with the interval between flashes about 1 second, and the interval between successive signals at least 10 seconds.
expected_points: Rule 34(b).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: In a narrow channel, when one vessel overtakes another and the overtaking vessel intends to overtake on the overtaken vessel's port side, what signal is given, and by whom?
gold_answer: The overtaking vessel sounds two prolonged blasts followed by two short blasts; the vessel to be overtaken, if in agreement, sounds one prolonged, one short, one prolonged, one short blast.
expected_points: Rule 34(c)(i)-(ii), read with Rule 9(e).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What signal may a vessel use to attract the attention of another vessel, per Rule 36?
gold_answer: Any light or sound signal that cannot be mistaken for any signal authorised elsewhere in the Rules, or she may direct the beam of her searchlight in the direction of the danger, in such a way as not to embarrass any vessel.
expected_points: Rule 36.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What Rule governs distress signals and where are they specified in detail?
gold_answer: Rule 37 states that when a vessel is in distress and requires assistance she shall use or exhibit the signals described in Annex IV.
expected_points: Rule 37, cross-referencing Annex IV.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: Vessel A gives one short blast while altering to starboard in a crossing situation. Vessel B, the stand-on vessel, does not intend to alter course. Must B respond with a whistle signal?
gold_answer: Not necessarily with a manoeuvring signal, since B is not herself altering course or operating astern propulsion; B should only sound the Rule 34(d) doubt/danger signal if she fails to understand A's intentions or doubts that A's action is sufficient.
expected_points: Whistle signals under Rule 34(a) are given when a vessel herself takes the described action, not as an automatic reply.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: Vessel A sees another vessel take an action she does not understand and is unsure it is sufficient to avoid collision. What must she immediately do?
gold_answer: Sound the danger signal: at least five short and rapid blasts on the whistle (and may supplement with at least five short and rapid flashes of a light).
expected_points: Rule 34(d) is mandatory ('shall'), not optional, once doubt/misunderstanding arises.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: Distinguish the meaning of 'one prolonged blast' under Rule 34(e) (bend signal) from 'one prolonged blast' under Rule 35(a) (fog signal for a vessel underway and making way).
gold_answer: They are the same physical signal (a single prolonged blast) but carry different meanings depending on context: under Rule 34(e) it warns of a blind bend/obstruction in a channel (any visibility), while under Rule 35(a) it is the periodic (every ≤2 min) position/identity signal of a power-driven vessel making way in restricted visibility.
expected_points: Context (narrow channel bend vs. restricted-visibility fog signalling) disambiguates the identical sound pattern.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: Why does a vessel 100 metres or more in length require a gong in addition to a bell?
gold_answer: So that the forward bell (anchor signal) and after gong (Rule 35(f) requires the gong sounded immediately after the bell in the after part) can be distinguished, helping other vessels judge the anchored vessel's length/orientation and position in restricted visibility.
expected_points: Rule 33(a) equipment requirement supports the Rule 35(f) signal procedure for large anchored vessels.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: How many flashes of light, if used, correspond to the whistle signal for 'I am altering my course to starboard'?
gold_answer: One flash.
expected_points: Rule 34(b) - flashes mirror the number of short blasts.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: What is the minimum visible range required for the optional manoeuvring/warning light under Rule 34(b)?
gold_answer: 5 nautical miles.
expected_points: Rule 34(b).

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: Under Rule 34(c), what identifies an overtaking-agreement whistle exchange as distinct from ordinary Rule 34(a) manoeuvring signals?
gold_answer: It uses prolonged blasts combined with short blasts in a specific pattern (two prolonged + one/two short from the overtaker; prolonged-short-prolonged-short in reply) rather than the simple 1/2/3 short-blast patterns used for ordinary course/astern-propulsion signals.
expected_points: This distinct pattern avoids confusion with ordinary Rule 34(a) manoeuvring signals.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: A whistle blast lasts 3 seconds. Does it qualify as a 'short blast' or 'prolonged blast' under Rule 32?
gold_answer: Neither precisely - a short blast is about 1 second and a prolonged blast is 4-6 seconds; a 3-second blast falls outside both defined categories and should not be relied upon as a compliant signal.
expected_points: Exam questions sometimes test the boundary values (1 second vs. 4-6 seconds) defined in Rule 32.

question: What is the general purpose of Rule 38?
gold_answer: To permit permanent exemptions for vessels whose keels were laid, or which were at a corresponding stage of construction, before the 1972 Rules (or later amendments) entered into force, from full compliance with certain light/shape/sound-signal requirements, for specified transitional periods or permanently in some cases.
expected_points: Rule 38 is a grandfathering/transitional provision, not a general loophole for modern vessels.

question: Under Rule 38, what is exempted 'permanently' regarding the positioning of lights, for existing vessels unable to fully comply?
gold_answer: The repositioning of lights as a result of conversion from Imperial to metric units and rounding off measurement figures is exempted permanently.
expected_points: Rule 38(a).

question: Do exemptions under Rule 38 apply to newly built vessels?
gold_answer: No - Rule 38 exemptions apply only to vessels the keels of which were laid, or which were at a corresponding stage of construction, before the relevant Rules or amendments entered into force; new vessels must fully comply.
expected_points: Rule 38 preamble.

question: Rule 38(c) concerns the repositioning of which lights, and for what exemption period from the date of entry into force of the Rules?
gold_answer: The repositioning of masthead lights resulting from the increase in minimum vertical separation prescribed, and other similar changes, with exemptions specified for periods such as 9 years from the date of entry into force.
expected_points: Rule 38(c)-(g) list specific time-limited exemptions for particular light/sound-signal changes introduced by amendment.

question: A vessel built decades ago claims a Rule 38 exemption to avoid fitting sidelights at all. Is this valid?
gold_answer: No - Rule 38 exemptions are narrow and specific (e.g., light repositioning/technical details due to amendments), not blanket exemptions from carrying required lights such as sidelights.
expected_points: Rule 38 exemptions must be read narrowly against their specific enumerated subjects.

question: Does compliance with a Rule 38 exemption remove a vessel's obligation to comply with the steering and sailing rules (Rules 4-19)?
gold_answer: No - Rule 38 concerns only technical light/shape/sound-signal equipment requirements; the steering and sailing rules apply to all vessels regardless of any Rule 38 exemption.
expected_points: Rule 38 is limited to Part C/D technical compliance, not navigational conduct.

question: Which Part of the Rules does Rule 38 primarily grant exemptions from?
gold_answer: Primarily Part C (Lights and Shapes) and, to a lesser extent, sound signal appliance requirements under Part D/Annex III, concerning vessels built before certain amendment dates.
expected_points: Rule 38.

question: Why are Rule 38 exemptions time-limited or subject-limited rather than indefinite for all requirements?
gold_answer: To balance fairness to owners of older vessels (avoiding costly immediate retrofits) against the safety benefit of universal compliance, exemptions are narrowly scoped to specific technical changes and, in most cases, phased out after a defined transitional period.
expected_points: This reflects the IMO's general approach to phasing in safety-equipment amendments.

question: On a power-driven vessel 20 metres or more in length, where must masthead lights be positioned relative to the hull?
gold_answer: Placed as such a height above the hull that the forward masthead light is not less than 6 metres above the hull if the vessel's breadth exceeds 6 metres (with further formula-based minimums), and generally so that lower lights are shielded/visible in accordance with prescribed arcs.
expected_points: Annex I, Section 2 sets out detailed vertical positioning formulas for masthead lights based on breadth and length.

question: What is the minimum vertical separation between the forward and after masthead lights on a vessel 50 metres or more in length?
gold_answer: The after masthead light shall be at least 4.5 metres vertically higher than the forward one.
expected_points: Annex I, Section 2(a)(ii).

question: On a vessel with two masthead lights, how must they be horizontally spaced relative to each other?
gold_answer: The after masthead light shall be so placed that, when seen in conjunction with the forward light, it is clearly distinguishable as being at a different level, generally with adequate fore-and-aft separation so their differing heights are apparent from all relevant angles.
expected_points: Annex I §2 - exact spacing depends on vessel dimensions and geometry tables.

question: Where should sidelights be positioned on a power-driven vessel with two masthead lights?
gold_answer: At a height above the hull not greater than three-quarters of that of the forward masthead light, and not so low as to be interfered with by deck lights.
expected_points: Annex I, Section 3.

question: May sidelights be combined into a single lantern and where is it typically carried?
gold_answer: Yes, on a vessel less than 20 metres in length, sidelights may be combined in one lantern carried on the fore-and-aft centreline of the vessel, except that on vessels less than 12 metres they may also be placed as close as practicable to that line.
expected_points: Annex I §3(b).

question: What is the minimum requirement for the horizontal sectors of lights (in terms of intensity) at the boundaries of their prescribed arcs?
gold_answer: Lights shall be so fixed that at the prescribed arc boundaries (e.g., 112.5 degrees, 225 degrees) they show the minimum required intensity down to at least 1 degree inside the prescribed arc, with a smooth reduction of intensity permitted within 5 degrees of the boundary such that it is practically extinguished at 5 degrees outside.
expected_points: Annex I, Section 9 governs horizontal sectors and permissible intensity cut-off characteristics.

question: What is the minimum intensity requirement basis for navigation lights under Annex I?
gold_answer: Lights must have the luminous intensity calculated by a formula relating to the minimum range of visibility prescribed in Rule 22, using a specified background/adaptation illumination standard (0.2 microlux background luminance).
expected_points: Annex I, Section 8 (luminous intensity formula).

question: What colour specifications (chromaticity) apply to navigation lights under Annex I?
gold_answer: Colours must fall within chromaticity boundaries specified by the CIE (International Commission on Illumination) for white, red, green and yellow navigation lights.
expected_points: Annex I, Section 7.

question: What is the vertical sector requirement for navigation lights (other than all-round lights) as installed on a vessel underway on an even keel?
gold_answer: The lights must ensure at least the required minimum intensity at all angles from 5 degrees above to 5 degrees below the horizontal.
expected_points: Annex I, Section 9 (vertical sectors).

question: What does Annex I say about the location of directional/manoeuvring lights and all-round lights used with sound signals (Rule 34)?
gold_answer: They shall be positioned to avoid interference from other lights and be shielded or positioned so as to prevent confusion with the vessel's other navigation lights.
expected_points: Annex I, Section 12 addresses manoeuvring light placement.

question: What details does Annex I give about the diamond, ball, cone, and cylinder shapes used as day signals?
gold_answer: It specifies minimum dimensions (e.g., a ball shall have a diameter of not less than 0.6 metre; a cone shall have a base diameter of not less than 0.6 metre and a height equal to its diameter), colour (black), and vertical spacing between multiple shapes (not less than 1.5 metres apart, with the lowest shape not less than 4 metres above the hull on vessels over 20 m).
expected_points: Annex I, Section 6 (Shapes).

question: What is specified about the colour of shapes under Annex I?
gold_answer: Shapes shall be black.
expected_points: Annex I, Section 6.

question: Why does Annex I mandate minimum vertical separation between the two masthead lights of a large vessel?
gold_answer: So that an observer can distinguish the forward and after masthead lights as being at different heights, which, combined with their relative horizontal alignment, helps another vessel judge the observed vessel's heading/aspect (e.g., whether she is approaching head-on, crossing, or moving away).
expected_points: This supports the practical application of Rule 14/15 aspect determination at night.

question: For small vessels (under 20 m), does Annex I permit any relaxation of the strict masthead light height formulas?
gold_answer: Yes - Annex I provides adjusted, generally lower, minimum height requirements and combined-lantern options for smaller vessels (e.g., under 12 m and under 20 m categories) reflecting their different construction and lower freeboard.
expected_points: Annex I §2(f) and related sub-sections tailor requirements by vessel size.

question: What governs the screening of sidelights to prevent them from being seen across the bow?
gold_answer: Sidelights shall be fitted with matt black inboard screens sufficient to prevent the lights from being seen across the bow (i.e., the green light not visible from the port side and vice versa) at the prescribed cutoff.
expected_points: Annex I, Section 4 (Screens).

question: What is the minimum height above the hull for sidelights on a vessel less than 20 metres?
gold_answer: Not less than 1 metre above the gunwale, generally, subject to the vessel's specific dimensions and combined-lantern provisions.
expected_points: Annex I §3(a).

question: Must the two masthead lights of a large vessel be visible from directly astern?
gold_answer: No - masthead lights show only the 225-degree forward arc; they are not intended to be visible from astern.
expected_points: Annex I read with Rule 21(a).

question: What is the purpose of the intensity formula in Annex I Section 8?
gold_answer: To ensure each type/category of navigation light achieves at least the minimum range of visibility required by Rule 22 under a standard reference background luminance.
expected_points: Annex I §8.

question: Where should the all-round light for a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre be positioned relative to other lights, per Annex I general siting principles?
gold_answer: Where it can best be seen, positioned to avoid being obscured by the vessel's structure and to minimise confusion with other prescribed lights.
expected_points: Annex I general siting principles, Sections 2-3 and 9.

question: How many degrees apart, horizontally, must the day shapes (e.g., ball-diamond-ball for RAM) typically be positioned to remain visible around the vessel?
gold_answer: They are mounted vertically (not horizontally spaced) and must be clearly visible from all directions given their all-round black silhouette, which is why they are shown one above another rather than side by side.
expected_points: Annex I §6 on vertical shape arrangement.

question: What does Annex I say about supplementary/non-required lights that might impair the proper lights?
gold_answer: They must not be of such a character as to be mistaken for a prescribed light, impair its distinctive character or range, or interfere with the proper lookout.
expected_points: Rule 20(b), reinforced by Annex I light siting/technical provisions.

question: What minimum diameter is specified for a ball shape used as a day signal?
gold_answer: Not less than 0.6 metre.
expected_points: Annex I §6(a).

question: What is the minimum vertical distance apart for two or three shapes displayed in a vertical line?
gold_answer: Not less than 1.5 metres apart.
expected_points: Annex I §6(c).

question: At what minimum height above the hull should the lowest of a vertical line of shapes be carried, on a vessel of 20 metres or more in length?
gold_answer: Not less than 4 metres above the hull.
expected_points: Annex I §6(c).

question: What technical standard governs the exact chromaticity (colour boundaries) of navigation lights?
gold_answer: The boundaries recommended by the CIE (International Commission on Illumination), as set out in Annex I Section 7.
expected_points: Annex I §7.

question: To which vessels does Annex II apply?
gold_answer: Vessels engaged in fishing in close proximity to one another, in addition to the lights prescribed in Rule 26.
expected_points: Annex II, Section 1.

question: What additional lights may vessels engaged in trawling (trawlers) exhibit when shooting, hauling, or when their net has come fast upon an obstruction?
gold_answer: Two all-round white lights in a vertical line, shown to indicate the direction toward which she is shooting/hauling her net or that her gear is fast on an obstruction.
expected_points: Annex II §3-4 describes specific white-light combinations for shooting, hauling, and fast-on-obstruction states.

question: What signal indicates a trawler is shooting her net, per Annex II?
gold_answer: A white light showing forward and one other white light in the direction of the sidelight nearest the outlying gear or another combination as prescribed - specifically, two all-round white lights in a vertical line signal 'shooting nets' when accompanied by an all-round white light indicating the relevant direction (exact configuration set out in Annex II §3(a)).
expected_points: Annex II, Section 3, describes signals for trawlers working in a fleet.

question: What signal indicates a trawler's net has come fast upon an obstruction, per Annex II?
gold_answer: Four all-round white lights in a vertical line, or the equivalent day/other prescribed indication, to signal the net has become fast on an obstruction.
expected_points: Annex II §4.

question: What additional signals apply to purse seiners fishing in close proximity to one another?
gold_answer: A purse seiner may exhibit two all-round yellow lights in a vertical line, flashing alternately every second with equal duration, to indicate she is hampered by her gear.
expected_points: Annex II §5.

question: Why does Annex II provide supplementary signals beyond the Rule 26 fishing-vessel lights?
gold_answer: Because vessels fishing together as a fleet need to communicate specific operational states (shooting, hauling, fast on an obstruction, hampered by purse-seine gear) to one another to coordinate manoeuvring safely, which the general Rule 26 lights alone do not convey.
expected_points: Annex II supplements, and does not replace, Rule 26.

question: Are Annex II signals a substitute for the Rule 26 fishing vessel lights, or additional to them?
gold_answer: Additional to them - Annex II signals are shown in addition to the lights prescribed by Rule 26.
expected_points: Annex II §1.

question: A trawler operating within a fishing fleet shows a specific combination of additional white lights signalling 'hauling her net'. Should nearby trawlers alter their approach based on this signal?
gold_answer: Yes - nearby vessels should take this signal into account, giving the hauling vessel appropriate room, since her net is being retrieved and her manoeuvrability may be affected differently than while freely trawling.
expected_points: The purpose of Annex II signals is precisely to enable this kind of coordinated situational awareness among fishing fleet vessels.

question: What does the yellow flashing-light signal on a purse seiner specifically warn nearby vessels about?
gold_answer: That she is hampered by her purse-seine gear and has restricted ability to manoeuvre as a result, so other vessels should keep clear/give her room accordingly.
expected_points: Annex II §5.

question: Does Annex II apply to a single fishing vessel operating alone, far from other fishing vessels?
gold_answer: No - by its terms, Annex II concerns additional signals for vessels engaged in fishing in close proximity to one another (i.e., fleet operations); a lone fishing vessel need only comply with Rule 26.
expected_points: Annex II Section 1's scope is limited to close-proximity fleet fishing operations.

question: What general colour is used for Annex II supplementary trawler signals (as distinct from purse seiner signals)?
gold_answer: White, all-round lights, in various vertical-line combinations depending on the operational state; purse seiner supplementary signals, by contrast, use yellow.
expected_points: Trawler additional signals = white; purse seiner additional signal = yellow flashing.

question: What frequency range must a whistle operate within, per Annex III?
gold_answer: Between 70 and 700 Hz.
expected_points: Annex III, Section 1(b).

question: What determines the required minimum sound pressure level / audibility range of a whistle?
gold_answer: It depends on the vessel's length category, with specified 1/3-octave band levels at 1 metre and corresponding audibility ranges (e.g., roughly 2 nm for vessels 200 m or more, down to about 0.5 nm for small vessels under 20 m), as tabulated in Annex III.
expected_points: Annex III, Section 1(c) provides the table linking vessel length, frequency range, and required audibility range.

question: What is the required audibility range for the whistle of a vessel 200 metres or more in length?
gold_answer: Approximately 2 nautical miles.
expected_points: Annex III §1(c)(i) (vessels ≥ 200 m).

question: What is the required audibility range for the whistle of a vessel less than 20 metres in length?
gold_answer: Approximately 0.5 nautical mile.
expected_points: Annex III §1(c)(iv) (vessels < 20 m).

question: What does Annex III require regarding a vessel fitted with whistles at a distance apart of more than 100 metres?
gold_answer: Only one whistle shall be used for giving manoeuvring and warning signals; both may be used for giving fog signals.
expected_points: Annex III, Section 2.

question: What requirements does Annex III place on bell/gong construction?
gold_answer: A bell or gong (or other device with similar sound characteristics) shall be constructed so as to produce a sound pressure level of not less than a specified minimum at 1 metre; bells shall have a minimum diameter based on vessel length.
expected_points: Annex III, Section 3.

question: What is the minimum mouth diameter for a bell on a vessel 20 metres or more (but under 100 m) in length?
gold_answer: Approximately 300 mm.
expected_points: Annex III §3.

question: May a vessel use an approved substitute means (e.g., electronic apparatus) to produce bell/gong/whistle sound signals?
gold_answer: Yes, provided it is capable of manual operation as well and is otherwise compliant with the required sound characteristics.
expected_points: Annex III, Section 4.

question: Why does Annex III scale required whistle frequency and audibility range inversely with vessel length (larger vessels use lower frequency, longer range)?
gold_answer: Larger vessels need to be heard from a greater distance given their size, speed, and manoeuvring constraints, and lower-frequency sound travels further with less atmospheric attenuation, matching the propagation requirement to the vessel's practical stopping/manoeuvring needs.
expected_points: This mirrors the same length-based logic used for light visibility ranges under Rule 22/Annex I.

question: A 250-metre vessel's whistle frequency is measured at 550 Hz. Is this within the Annex III requirement?
gold_answer: Yes, provided it falls within the 70-700 Hz general range and meets the specific fundamental frequency band appropriate to her length category and required sound pressure level; large vessels typically use lower frequencies within this range.
expected_points: Annex III §1(b)-(c) specifies both the overall frequency band and length-specific sub-ranges.

question: Does Annex III govern the design of the whistle, the bell/gong, or both?
gold_answer: Both - it prescribes technical characteristics for whistles (Section 1-2) and for bell/gong sound signalling appliances (Section 3), plus alternative approved apparatus (Section 4).
expected_points: Annex III covers all sound signal appliances referenced in Rule 33.

question: What does Annex IV(2) prohibit and require regarding use of the listed distress signals?
gold_answer: It prohibits the use or exhibition of any of the Annex IV signals except to indicate distress and need of assistance, and prohibits the use of any signal that may be confused with them.
expected_points: Annex IV(2) - misuse of distress signals is itself a violation.

question: What does Annex IV(3) note about supplementary distress-related guidance?
gold_answer: Attention is drawn to relevant sections of the International Code of Signals, the IAMSAR Manual, and the following additional signals for use by aircraft engaged in coordinating search and rescue.
expected_points: Annex IV(3) cross-references other maritime/aviation SAR signalling guidance.

question: A stand-on vessel decides to take avoiding action under Rule 17(a)(ii) in a crossing situation, with sea room available, and the give-way vessel is on her port bow. In which direction should she generally avoid altering?
gold_answer: If circumstances allow, she should avoid altering course to port for a vessel on her own port side; she should prefer starboard alteration or speed reduction.
expected_points: Rule 17(c). This mirrors the restricted-visibility caution in Rule 19(d) but applies specifically to the in-sight crossing case.

question: Why does Rule 8(f) exist for a vessel that is 'not to impede' another (e.g., crossing a TSS lane, or a small craft near a channel-bound vessel)?
gold_answer: To ensure such a vessel takes early action to leave sufficient sea room and does not force the right-of-way vessel into a late, reactive manoeuvre, while clarifying that if risk of collision nonetheless develops, the normal steering/sailing rule obligations (e.g., Section II give-way duties) still fully apply.
expected_points: Rule 8(f) bridges the 'not to impede' concept used in Rules 9/10/18 with the general good-seamanship obligations of Rule 8.

question: A 9-metre open motorboat underway at night shows a single all-round white light only. Is this compliant?
gold_answer: Yes, provided her maximum speed does not exceed 7 knots per the relevant provision for small vessels (Rule 23(d)(i) allows a vessel under 7 metres, max speed not exceeding 7 knots, to show simply an all-round white light and, if practicable, sidelights); for a 9-metre vessel, Rule 23(c) instead permits an all-round white light in lieu of masthead light and sternlight for vessels under 12 metres generally.
expected_points: Rule 23(c)-(d) provide tiered simplified lighting options for small power-driven vessels.

question: Compare the obligations of Rule 17 (stand-on vessel duties, applicable when in sight) to Rule 19 (restricted visibility). Why can a vessel not simply 'stand on' in fog the way she might in clear weather?
gold_answer: Rule 17's stand-on concept depends on visual confirmation that the give-way vessel is aware of and responding to the situation, which is unavailable in restricted visibility; Rule 19 therefore imposes mutual, proactive avoiding-action duties on all vessels detected only by radar, without a passive 'hold course and speed' role.
expected_points: This contrast is one of the most frequently tested conceptual distinctions in COLREG exams.

question: Why does Annex I require a minimum vertical separation between a vessel's two masthead lights only on vessels above a certain length?
gold_answer: Smaller vessels have limited mast height and structural capacity to achieve large vertical separations, and their generally shorter length/lower speed reduces the practical need for the same degree of aspect-differentiation precision required for large, fast vessels at greater ranges.
expected_points: Annex I scales its technical requirements to vessel size throughout, balancing safety benefit against practicability.

section_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals
question: A sailing vessel underway in fog sounds one prolonged followed by two short blasts every two minutes. Is this compliant with Rule 35?
gold_answer: Yes - Rule 35(c) prescribes exactly this signal (one prolonged plus two short blasts, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes) for, among others, a sailing vessel underway.
expected_points: Rule 35(c) groups sailing vessels with NUC, RAM, CBD, fishing, and towing/pushing vessels underway for this common fog signal.

question: Two power-driven vessels are approaching such that each sees the other fine on her own bow, with a very small (a few degrees) relative bearing offset from dead ahead. Should this be treated as head-on or crossing?
gold_answer: It should be treated as head-on (Rule 14) - Rule 14(c) requires that if there is any doubt whether a head-on situation exists, it shall be assumed that it does, and a near-dead-ahead sighting with only a slight offset falls within this doubt.
expected_points: This prevents mariners from exploiting small bearing offsets to claim a crossing (single give-way) situation instead of the mutual head-on obligation.

question: A vessel engaged in diving operations from a small craft, too small to exhibit the full Rule 27(b) RAM lights/shapes, displays the rigid replica of the International Code flag 'A' ('Alpha'). Is this an internationally recognised alternative?
gold_answer: The 'Alpha' flag is widely used and recognised in many jurisdictions/practice to indicate a diver down, but it is not itself a Rule 27 light/shape substitute under COLREG; where practicable, small RAM vessels engaged in diving should still comply as closely as possible with Rule 27(b), and mariners should be aware that the 'Alpha' flag signals a diving operation as an internationally recognised caution regardless.
expected_points: This tests awareness that some widely used maritime signals (like the rigid 'Alpha' flag) exist alongside, but are distinct from, the formal COLREG light/shape scheme.

question: A vessel wants to anchor in a narrow channel to wait for a berth. Is this permitted under Rule 9(g)?
gold_answer: Only if circumstances of the case do not admit avoiding it - Rule 9(g) requires every vessel to avoid anchoring in a narrow channel if circumstances allow avoidance; waiting for a berth is not itself an exception, and she should seek to anchor outside the channel if practicable.
expected_points: Rule 9(g) sets a strong presumption against anchoring in narrow channels.

question: A vessel in genuine difficulty fires a single red flare and then, an hour later unrelated to any emergency, fires a second red flare for a celebration. Is the second use compliant with Annex IV?
gold_answer: No - Annex IV(2) prohibits the use or exhibition of any distress signal except to indicate distress and need of assistance; using a recognised distress signal (such as a red flare) for a non-distress purpose is a violation.
expected_points: Annex IV(2) exists to preserve the reliability and credibility of distress signals for genuine emergencies.

question: Vessel A (power-driven) has Vessel B (power-driven) on her starboard side, bearing 10 degrees relative from dead ahead, with risk of collision, both in sight in clear weather. Which vessel is give-way and what must she do?
gold_answer: Vessel A is give-way (Rule 15) and must take early and substantial action under Rule 16 to keep well clear of B, normally altering to starboard to pass under B's stern; B is stand-on and must keep her course and speed under Rule 17(a)(i), acting only under Rule 17(a)(ii)/(b) if A fails to act appropriately.
expected_points: A relative bearing of 10 degrees to starboard (within 0-112.5 degrees, not an overtaking geometry) places B in the sector that makes A the give-way vessel under Rule 15.
